# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, conferring a four- to fivefold increased risk [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC) with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) substantially reduces thromboembolic risk but carries an inherent bleeding hazard and is contraindicated or poorly tolerated in many patients [2,3]. Because approximately 90% of thrombi in nonvalvular AF originate in the left atrial appendage (LAA), mechanical exclusion of this structure has emerged as a compelling alternative to lifelong anticoagulation [4]. Percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) provides a device-based strategy for stroke prevention in selected patients.

## Rationale and Devices

The LAA is an embryological remnant of the primordial left atrium with complex and variable morphology, classified into "chicken wing," "cactus," "windsock," and "cauliflower" types, which influence procedural planning [5]. Surgical LAA exclusion was historically performed during cardiac surgery with inconsistent results, motivating dedicated percutaneous approaches [6].

Two device families dominate clinical practice. Endocardial occluders, including the Watchman and Watchman FLX (Boston Scientific) and the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott), are deployed transseptally to seal the LAA ostium [7,8]. The epicardial LARIAT system uses a combined endocardial-epicardial approach to ligate the appendage with a suture [9]. The PROTECT AF and PREVAIL trials established the evidence base for the Watchman device, while subsequent iterations improved sealing and reduced peri-device leak [10,11].

## Clinical Evidence

PROTECT AF randomized 707 patients with nonvalvular AF to Watchman or warfarin and demonstrated noninferiority for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, albeit with early procedural complications [10]. PREVAIL addressed safety concerns and confirmed improved procedural outcomes with operator experience [11]. A patient-level meta-analysis of these trials with five-year follow-up showed comparable stroke prevention and reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality compared with warfarin [12].

The PRAGUE-17 trial compared LAAC against DOACs in high-risk patients and found LAAC noninferior for major cardiovascular and bleeding events, extending the evidence into the DOAC era [13]. Registry data, including the EWOLUTION study and the US National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry, have confirmed high procedural success and favorable real-world safety profiles [14,15]. The Amulet IDE trial directly compared the Amplatzer Amulet with the Watchman, showing comparable effectiveness with differences in closure mechanism and leak rates [16].

## Patient Selection and Imaging

Current guidelines support LAAC primarily in patients with nonvalvular AF and elevated stroke risk who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation [17,18]. Risk stratification employs the CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores to balance thromboembolic and bleeding risks [19]. Multimodality imaging is central to procedural success. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and cardiac computed tomography enable accurate LAA sizing, exclusion of pre-existing thrombus, and device selection [20,21]. Intracardiac echocardiography is increasingly used as an alternative to TEE, facilitating procedures under conscious sedation [22].

## Procedural Considerations and Complications

LAAC is performed via transseptal puncture, ideally at an inferior-posterior position to optimize device coaxiality [23]. Major periprocedural complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, and vascular access complications, with rates declining as operator experience and device design improve [15,24]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 3–4% of patients and is associated with increased thromboembolic events, underscoring the importance of post-procedural surveillance imaging [25]. Peri-device leak, particularly larger residual flow, has also been linked to adverse outcomes [26].

## Antithrombotic Management

Post-implantation antithrombotic regimens have evolved. Initial protocols mandated warfarin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy, but contemporary practice frequently employs short-course DOACs or dual antiplatelet therapy, especially in patients with bleeding contraindications [27]. The optimal regimen remains an area of active investigation, with trials evaluating reduced or abbreviated antithrombotic strategies [28].

## Future Directions

Ongoing randomized trials, including CHAMPION-AF and OPTION, are comparing LAAC with DOACs in broader populations, potentially expanding indications beyond anticoagulation-ineligible patients [29]. Combined procedures, such as concomitant catheter ablation and LAAC, and refinements in device technology and imaging-guided deployment promise continued improvement [30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC is an established option for stroke prevention in patients with nonvalvular AF who cannot tolerate long-term anticoagulation. Robust randomized and registry data support its efficacy and safety, though challenges including device-related thrombus and peri-device leak persist. Forthcoming trials may broaden its role across the AF population.
